blocks.text: 1. Sentence Embeddings

blocks.alt: A sentence goes through a sentence encoder to produce a sentence vector

blocks.text: Sentence embeddings extend these word-level ideas up to whole sentences and passages, taking representation one level higher.
They represent an entire piece of text as a single dense vector, a different unit of representation than a word embedding.
2. Recapping The Preview
Sentence embeddings were briefly previewed in fastText as extending word-level ideas upward.
This topic gives that idea the full, dedicated treatment.
3. The Word Level Limitation

blocks.alt: Word embeddings have no whole-sentence meaning

blocks.text: Word2Vec, Skip-gram, GloVe, and fastText each produce one vector per word, but many real tasks need to compare or classify whole sentences instead.
A simple list of individual word vectors does not solve that on its own.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Task type","Best suited representation"],"rows":[["Per-word tasks, like tagging individual words","Word-level embeddings"],["Whole-sentence tasks, like similarity or search","Sentence embeddings"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Simple Averaging Baseline

blocks.alt: Word vector 1 and word vector 2 average into a sentence vector

blocks.text: The simplest baseline averages every word vector in a sentence together into one combined vector.
This is easy to compute, but it loses all word order information in the process.
5. Learned Sentence Encoders

blocks.alt: A sentence goes through a learned encoder to produce a sentence vector

blocks.text: Dedicated sentence encoder models learn much richer sentence vectors instead of relying on plain averaging.
They are trained specifically so that similar sentences end up with nearby vectors.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This training objective is why learned sentence encoders outperform the simple averaging baseline on most real tasks.

blocks.text: 6. Siamese Network Structure

blocks.alt: Sentence A and sentence B both go through a shared encoder

blocks.text: A common training setup encodes two sentences with the same shared encoder.
It then compares the two resulting vectors directly, adjusting the shared encoder based on how well that comparison matches the true label.
7. Recapping Cosine Similarity
Cosine similarity measures how closely two sentence vectors point in the same direction.
This is a standard way of scoring how semantically similar two sentences actually are, and it is used in the worked example below.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Similarity score","Interpretation"],"rows":[["Close to 1","Two sentences point in a similar direction, likely similar meaning"],["Close to 0","Two sentences point in unrelated directions, likely unrelated meaning"]]}

blocks.text: 8. Transformer Based Sentence Embeddings

blocks.alt: A transformer model produces pooled output, which becomes a sentence vector

blocks.text: Modern sentence embedding models build on transformer architectures.
They pool token-level representations together into a single sentence-level vector, a widely used modern approach.
9. Recognizing When Sentence Embeddings Are The Right Tool

blocks.alt: Needing whole-sentence meaning points toward sentence embeddings

blocks.text: When the task is comparing or searching whole sentences, sentence embeddings deliver exactly that.
For per-word tasks, individual word vectors as covered in Word Embeddings remain better suited.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates the simple averaging baseline and cosine similarity applied to comparing two short sentences.

code.content:
import math

# a simplified stand-in for real word vectors
word_vectors = {
    "cat": [0.9, 0.1], "dog": [0.8, 0.2], "sat": [0.1, 0.9],
    "mat": [0.2, 0.8], "ran": [0.15, 0.85], "park": [0.25, 0.75],
}

def average_vector(sentence, word_vectors):
    # the simple averaging baseline
    vectors = [word_vectors[w] for w in sentence.split() if w in word_vectors]
    dims = len(vectors[0])
    return [sum(v[d] for v in vectors) / len(vectors) for d in range(dims)]

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    # scores semantic closeness between two vectors
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    norm_a = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a))
    norm_b = math.sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b))
    return dot / (norm_a * norm_b)

sentence_a = "cat sat mat"
sentence_b = "dog ran park"

vec_a = average_vector(sentence_a, word_vectors)
vec_b = average_vector(sentence_b, word_vectors)

similarity = cosine_similarity(vec_a, vec_b)
print(f"Sentence A vector: {vec_a}")
print(f"Sentence B vector: {vec_b}")
print(f"\nCosine similarity: {similarity:.3f}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows two structurally similar sentences producing a high cosine similarity score, even using only the simple averaging baseline.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Sentence embeddings represent an entire sentence or passage as one single dense vector.
Word-level embeddings alone do not directly solve whole-sentence comparison or classification tasks.
A simple averaging baseline combines word vectors into one, but loses all word order information.
Dedicated sentence encoders learn richer vectors, trained so similar sentences end up nearby.
Siamese network structures use one shared encoder to compare two sentences directly during training.
Cosine similarity measures how closely two sentence vectors point in the same direction.
Modern sentence embedding models build on transformer architectures, pooling tokens into one vector.
Sentence embeddings suit whole-sentence tasks; word-level embeddings suit per-word tasks.
Next up: Positional Embeddings, addressing how order information gets reintroduced into these representations.
